program: Before You Deploy an AI Agent: Executive Decision Workshop
form: AUTHOR-REVIEWED EDUCATIONAL BLUEPRINT FOR FUTURE HTML, NOT CUSTOMER EVALUATION

scenarios.title: The pilot can change supplier payment details
scenarios.riskMoment: A purchasing AI agent passed functional demonstrations. Authorized repository analysis now establishes a source path from the agent through a tool handler to supplier bank-detail updates. Current effective IAM grants, approved delegated business choice, customer-side target enforcement and action outcomes have not been established.
scenarios.outcome: A bounded initial pilot may be considered only within independently controlled operations. Payment-detail mutation cannot be represented as approved or safely protected without its specific prerequisites.

fivePlanes.requested: Documented business goal: draft purchase orders
fivePlanes.policyAuthorized: Not established for changes to banking instructions
fivePlanes.codeCapable: Source-qualified path to supplier bank-detail write established

scenarios.executiveExposure: Unauthorized payment routing, supplier trust, treasury loss
responsibleOwners: Chief financial officer or delegated payment-control owner

questions.prompt: What can leadership responsibly conclude from the source-backed finding?
options: The system already changed a real supplier bank account.
The agent implementation contains a path that can reach a supplier banking write, but permission, authority and real execution remain unresolved.
Because runtime evidence is missing, no consequential action is possible.
questions.explanation: Qualified code reachability is valuable evidence of a potential business consequence. It neither establishes effective deployment permission nor proves a completed payment change.
badReasons: A code path is not an observed mutation.
Missing runtime evidence cannot be converted into proof the action did not occur.

questions.prompt: What minimum additional proof is relevant before expanding to bank-detail changes?
options: A good model benchmark and supplier satisfaction survey.
An executive email saying the pilot is promising.
An action-specific approved policy and delegated choice, the deployed principal's relevant effective permission, and customer-side mediation/target evidence appropriate to the action.
questions.explanation: The open question is who can authorize a sensitive choice and what actually limits or records it. Source capability is only one plane.
badReasons: Performance does not bind authorization.
Business interest is not a scoped technical permission or valid operational control.

questions.prompt: Which operating decision fits the evidence and preserves business progress?
options: Permit a narrow pilot only for approved low-consequence operations, with bank-detail changes out of scope until their gates are evidenced and separately approved.
Approve all capabilities because the functional test passed.
Reject the whole AI investment permanently solely because IAM evidence is absent.
questions.explanation: A restricted pilot may be an option if those operations have their own adequate controls. The sensitive mutation is not silently included. Human approval is not enforcement.
badReasons: A working demo is not sufficient authority.
Evidence gaps can call for conditions or restrictions rather than permanent rejection.

questions.prompt: How should the executive record the remaining risk?
options: Mark the agent safe and leave acceptance implicit.
Assign an accountable owner, state excluded operations and unresolved evidence, define expiry/review triggers and record a scoped decision subject to organizational risk tolerance.
Treat the generated assurance PDF as a substitute for treasury approval.
questions.explanation: Risk acceptance is an accountable human decision for a named scope, with conditions and re-review triggers, never a blanket assurance score.
badReasons: Unrecorded risk acceptance is not defensible.
An assurance report does not replace payment governance.

sourcePrompts: Confirm repository commit and exact handler/action target
Provide policy envelope and delegated decision owner
Bind the deployed service principal and effective grants for the action
Provide target-side enforcement/outcome records if claiming intervention
Define pilot exclusions, expiry and owner
scenarios.recommendedDecision: Scoped pilot for unrelated permitted tasks, sensitive payment mutation not approved
scenarios.decisionBoundary: A workshop recommendation is educational and not a persisted HAIEC deployment decision.

scenarios.title: A third-party AI assistant wants customer-system access
scenarios.riskMoment: A vendor provides a current SOC 2 report and model security test results, and asks for an enterprise CRM connection. The enterprise has not assessed the integration's tool scopes, tenant-to-subject binding, resource ownership checks or outbound data paths.
scenarios.outcome: Vendor attestations and model tests can inform diligence, but they do not independently establish this integration's access boundaries or business consequences.

fivePlanes.requested: Proposed scope: answer authorized customer support questions
fivePlanes.policyAuthorized: Internal data-use/role policy not yet mapped to the vendor integration
fivePlanes.effectivelyGranted: Token and resource-specific permissions not assessed
fivePlanes.codeCapable: Vendor code and API call paths not available to this exercise
fivePlanes.observed: No permitted tenant-scoped test or live witness provided

scenarios.executiveExposure: Customer confidentiality, cross-tenant data access, unintended CRM writes

questions.prompt: What do the vendor's SOC 2 report and model benchmark establish for this specific CRM integration?
options: They certify the agent's exact tenant isolation and allowed tool actions.
They prove the vendor cannot leak customer data.
They contribute relevant diligence evidence but do not on their own establish this integration's principal, object-level scope, tool paths or observed outcomes.
questions.explanation: Organizational controls and model tests are different from the exact permissions, identity joins and data flows of the proposed customer integration.
badReasons: The report does not substitute for the actual integration authorization chain.
Safety benchmarks do not independently prove private data containment.

questions.prompt: Which request is most useful before production CRM access?
options: A vendor-controlled demonstration using unrestricted real customer records.
A documented integration scope, effective token permissions, trusted tenant/subject-to-resource checks, data egress controls and an agreed authorized negative test.
A signed statement that the model follows a prompt instructing it to protect data.
questions.explanation: The organization needs to qualify the integration's sensitive access boundary, not merely obtain persuasive assurances.
badReasons: Production private data should not be the default unbounded test material.
Instructions alone are not independent access controls.

questions.prompt: What is the most defensible next step?
options: Proceed with isolated, least-privilege synthetic-data evaluation and defer sensitive CRM access until evidence and approvals are adequate.
Enable broad CRM write and export permissions to save integration time.
Declare the product unusable forever because the vendor cannot share all source code.
questions.explanation: The decision can preserve learning progress with controlled fixtures while withholding sensitive production privileges. Access to unavailable vendor source remains a stated limitation.
badReasons: Unrestricted access outruns the verified scope.
Black-box limits require scoped risk treatment, not a fabricated clean or unsafe verdict.

questions.prompt: Who must own the integration decision and what must be recorded?
options: The vendor alone, because it built the product.
Nobody, because an existing attestation transfers responsibility.
The enterprise's authorized data owner and risk/security reviewers, with allowed APIs/data, exclusions, test results, expiry and review trigger.
questions.explanation: Vendor evidence can support due diligence, but accepting access risks is an enterprise decision with explicit scope and accountable people.
badReasons: The customer still owns its tenant access decision.
Third-party certifications do not transfer all operational accountability.

sourcePrompts: Authorized synthetic negative test and result
Data owner review and access recertification date
scenarios.recommendedDecision: Proceed only to a synthetic-data least-privilege evaluation until sensitive access is justified
scenarios.decisionBoundary: Do not claim vendor source analysis, observed cross-tenant exploit or certification when none exists.

scenarios.title: The rollout approval belongs to an older release
scenarios.sector: Telecom or other high-impact operational agent
scenarios.riskMoment: A network operations agent has an existing scoped human approval and historical assurance ALLOW for release A. Release B adds a tool path, the operating policy changed, and an event states that a request was accepted by a provider. There is no exact correlated target-system confirmation of the new operation.
scenarios.outcome: Previously valid assurance and human approval may be stale. Provider acknowledgment is not independent proof the native target action was applied or blocked.

fivePlanes.requested: Release B proposes an additional network-control operation
fivePlanes.policyAuthorized: Older policy version was approved; current binding changed
fivePlanes.effectivelyGranted: New tool permission not independently assessed
fivePlanes.codeCapable: Release A evaluated; release B added an unassessed source path
fivePlanes.observed: Provider acceptance event exists; target effect not qualified

scenarios.executiveExposure: Unauthorized network state change, customer outage, altered operational configuration

questions.prompt: Does the existing historical ALLOW and approval cover release B automatically?
options: Yes, an ALLOW result is a permanent permission for all future agent versions.
No, a policy/release change requires the current approval/evaluation binding to be rechecked before treating the old scope as current.
Yes, when the same model provider is used.
questions.explanation: HAIEC's deployment-decision contract explicitly distinguishes current approvals from expired, stale-policy and stale-evaluation records. U5 ALLOW is not deployment approval.
badReasons: An assurance disposition is bounded in time and scope.
A model vendor label does not preserve code, tool, policy or execution identity.

questions.prompt: What does the provider acceptance event prove?
options: A qualified provider accepted a request, but the native target operation's applied effect remains unestablished.
The new network configuration definitely changed at the target.
The enforcement middleware definitely blocked the operation.
questions.explanation: Dispatch, provider acknowledgment, applied-at-target and independent effect evidence are separate claims with their own source requirements.
badReasons: Acknowledgment is not a target witness.
An acceptance event does not imply a block.

questions.prompt: What decision best protects operations without discarding all prior work?
options: Expand automatically because the previous source report was reproducible.
Disable all telecom AI indefinitely because the new release has unknowns.
Do not extend the old approval to the new operation; require fresh scoped evaluation, policy/permission binding, accountable approval and target-specific evidence before higher-impact use.
questions.explanation: Unchanged low-risk approved work may be governed separately; a new consequential operation should not borrow an old approval without new evidence.
badReasons: Repeatability of an older evaluation does not make it current.
Permanent shutdown is not the only proportionate response to an evidence gap.

questions.prompt: What should the decision memo require if a narrower rollout is considered?
options: A green icon on the monitoring dashboard, regardless of producer coverage.
Specified permitted operations, target guard owner, telemetry/source coverage, failure response, renewal trigger and a reviewable decision expiry.
No review date because the project was previously approved.
questions.explanation: Residual risk treatment needs an explicit operating envelope and review trigger. Configured monitoring without source freshness and target checks is not verified protection.
badReasons: Monitoring configuration is not equivalent to qualified coverage.
Prior approval can become stale or expired.

sourcePrompts: Pin exact release A and B source/build/deployment identities
Bind current policy digest and exact approval request version
Assess changed tool and IAM access for new operation
Correlate native target outcome with exact dispatched action
Set stop condition and human reapproval trigger
scenarios.recommendedDecision: No automatic expansion; reassess new operation and obtain current scoped approval
scenarios.decisionBoundary: No educational answer can directly set real runtime entitlement, native guard status or customer deployment decision.
